title: Common Multiple of All Values
description: Return the smallest positive integer that is divisible by every element of `nums`.

examples.explanation: 12 is the smallest number divisible by 4, 6 and 3.
A single value is its own answer.

constraints: The answer fits in a 32-bit signed integer

title: Prime Factors With Multiplicity
description: Return how many prime factors `n` has when each prime is counted as many times as it divides `n` (so 12 = 2 * 2 * 3 has three). Return 0 for `n = 1`.

examples.explanation: 97 is prime, so it has a single prime factor.

title: Count of Divisors
description: Return the number of positive integers that divide `n` exactly (including 1 and `n` itself).

examples.explanation: The divisors of 12 are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 and 12.
36 has the divisors 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 9, 12, 18 and 36.

constraints: All inputs are integers within the stated ranges

title: Abundant Numbers Up To N
description: A number is abundant if the sum of its proper divisors (divisors smaller than itself) is greater than the number. Return how many abundant numbers lie in `[1, n]`.

examples.explanation: 12 is abundant (1+2+3+4+6 = 16), and so are 18 and 20.
No number below 12 is abundant.

constraints: All inputs are integers within the stated ranges

title: Self-Dividing Numbers Count
description: A number is self-dividing if it contains no digit 0 and is divisible by each of its own digits. Return how many self-dividing numbers are in `[1, n]`.

examples.explanation: 1 to 9 all qualify, plus 11, 12 and 15.
Only 1 qualifies.

constraints: All inputs are integers within the stated ranges

title: Mirror Binary Value
description: Write the positive integer `n` in binary without leading zeros, reverse that string, and return its value as an integer.

examples.explanation: 13 is 1101, which reversed is 1011 = 11.
8 is 1000, which reversed is 0001 = 1.

constraints: All inputs are integers within the stated ranges

title: Even Popcount Numbers
description: Return how many integers in `[0, n]` have an even number of 1 bits in their binary representation (0 has zero 1 bits).

examples.explanation: 0, 3, 5 and 6 have an even number of set bits.
Only 0 qualifies.

constraints: All inputs are integers within the stated ranges

title: Digit Sum in Another Base
description: Write `n` in base `k` and return the sum of its digits, with that sum given in base 10.

examples.explanation: 34 in base 6 is 54, and 5 + 4 = 9.
10 in base 10 has digits 1 and 0.

title: Round Up to Power of Two
description: Return the smallest power of two that is greater than or equal to `n`.

examples.explanation: 5 rounds up to 8.
16 is already a power of two.

constraints: All inputs are integers within the stated ranges

title: Pascal Entry Lookup
description: Return the binomial coefficient C(n, k): the number of ways to choose `k` items from `n` items, which is entry `k` of row `n` of Pascal's triangle (both 0-indexed).
constraints: All inputs are integers within the stated ranges

title: Exactly One Divisor Match
description: Count the integers in `[1, n]` that are divisible by exactly one of `a` and `b` (not both, not neither).

examples.explanation: The numbers 2, 3, 4, 8, 9 and 10 are divisible by exactly one of 2 and 3 (6 is divisible by both).
Every number is divisible by 1, and 2 is the only multiple of 2 that is... no other number qualifies.

title: Row With Most Ones
description: `a` is an `rows x cols` binary matrix stored row by row in a flat array (cell `(i, j)` is `a[i * cols + j]`). Return the index of the row with the most 1s; on ties return the smallest index.

examples.explanation: Row 1 has two 1s, more than row 0.
Both rows have one 1, so the smaller index wins.

title: Grid Border Sum
description: `a` is a `rows x cols` matrix stored row by row in a flat array. Return the sum of all cells on the outer border (first and last row, first and last column), counting each cell once.

examples.explanation: The border is every cell except the centre 5, so 45 - 5 = 40.
A 1 x 3 matrix is all border.

title: Strict Local Peaks in Grid
description: `a` is a `rows x cols` matrix stored row by row in a flat array. A cell is a peak if it is strictly greater than each of its existing up, down, left and right neighbours. Return the number of peak cells.

examples.explanation: The 9 and the 7 (right side) are peaks... the cells 9 and 8 are the only ones above all their neighbours.
A lone cell has no neighbours, so it is a peak.

title: Magic Square Verification
description: `a` holds an `n x n` matrix row by row. Return `true` if all `n` row sums, all `n` column sums and both main diagonal sums are the same value, otherwise `false`. Values need not be distinct.

examples.explanation: Every row, column and diagonal sums to 15.
Changing one cell breaks the equal sums.

title: Odd-Degree Vertices
description: An undirected simple graph has `n` vertices labelled `0..n-1`. `edges` lists undirected edges as consecutive pairs: edge `i` joins `edges[2i]` and `edges[2i+1]`. Return how many vertices have an odd number of incident edges.

examples.explanation: Vertices 1 and 3... vertices 0 and 3 have degree 1, vertices 1 and 2 have degree 2.
Every vertex of a triangle has degree 2.

title: Dead-End Nodes
description: A directed graph has `n` nodes labelled `0..n-1`. `edges` lists directed edges as consecutive pairs: edge `i` goes from `edges[2i]` to `edges[2i+1]`. Return the number of nodes with no outgoing edge.

examples.explanation: Nodes 2 and 3 have no outgoing edge.
With no edges every node is a dead end.

title: Bank Account Replay
description: An account starts at balance 0. `ops` is a list of operations stored as consecutive pairs `(type, amount)`: type 1 deposits `amount`; type 2 withdraws `amount` only if the balance is at least `amount`, otherwise the withdrawal is ignored. Return the final balance.

examples.explanation: Deposit 100, withdraw 30, then withdraw 50 leaves 20.
The withdrawal of 10 fails on an empty account, then 5 is deposited.

title: Bounded Queue Replay
description: A FIFO queue holds at most `cap` values. `ops` is a list of consecutive pairs `(type, x)`: type 1 enqueues `x` (ignored if the queue is full); type 2 dequeues the front (ignored if empty, and `x` is unused). Return `sum((i + 1) * v)` over the remaining values from front to back, using 0-based `i`, or 0 if the queue is empty.

examples.explanation: The third enqueue is dropped; after a dequeue the queue is [6], so the checksum is 6.
The queue ends as [7, 8], giving 7 + 16 = 23.

title: Tic-Tac-Toe Game Result
description: Players X and O alternate on a 3x3 board whose cells are numbered 0..8 row by row; X moves first, and `moves[i]` is the cell chosen on turn `i`. Return 1 if X has three in a row after the last move, 2 if O does, 0 if the board is full with no winner, and -1 if the game is not finished.

examples.explanation: X holds cells 0, 1 and 2 after the fifth move.
Three moves have been played and nobody has won yet.

constraints: All moves are distinct values in 0..8
No move is made after a player has already won

title: Day Number in the Year
description: Given a Gregorian calendar date `year`, `month`, `day`, return its position within the year, where 1 January is day 1. A year is a leap year if it is divisible by 4, except century years not divisible by 400.

examples.explanation: 31 + 28 days of January and February (2019 is not a leap year) plus 9 gives day 69.
In the leap year 2000, February has 29 days, so 1 March is day 61.

title: Leap Years Between
description: Return how many leap years lie in the inclusive range `[a, b]`. A year is a leap year if it is divisible by 4, except century years not divisible by 400.

examples.explanation: 1996, 2000 and 2004 are leap years (1900 is not).
2100 is a century year not divisible by 400.

constraints: All inputs are integers within the stated ranges

title: Pillow Holder After Seconds
description: `n` people stand in a line numbered 1 to `n`, and person 1 holds a pillow. Each second the pillow passes to the next person in the current direction, and the direction reverses whenever it reaches either end of the line. Return who holds the pillow after `t` seconds.

examples.explanation: The pillow goes 1, 2, 3, 4 over three seconds.
It goes 1, 2, 3, then back to 2, 1, 2.

title: Last Guest Candy Share
description: Candies are handed out to `people` guests standing in a row: 1 candy to the first guest, 2 to the second, and so on, one more each time and wrapping back to the first guest after the last. When fewer candies remain than the amount due, the current guest gets all remaining candies and distribution stops. Return the total candies received by the last guest.

examples.explanation: The guests get 1, 2, 3 and then the last 4 candies... [1,2,3,4] with the leftover going to the first guest, so the last guest gets 3.
One guest receives everything, 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10.

title: Euclid Division Steps
description: Running Euclid's algorithm on `(a, b)` repeats `(a, b) -> (b, a mod b)` until `b` becomes 0. Return how many such steps are performed.
constraints: All inputs are integers within the stated ranges

title: Reduced Fraction Total
description: Reduce the fraction `a / b` to lowest terms and return the sum of its numerator and denominator.

examples.explanation: 6/8 reduces to 3/4.
7/13 is already in lowest terms.

constraints: All inputs are integers within the stated ranges

title: Twin Prime Pairs
description: Twin primes are two primes that differ by exactly 2. Return how many pairs `(p, p + 2)` of twin primes have `p + 2 <= n`.

examples.explanation: The pairs are (3,5), (5,7) and (11,13).
The smallest pair (3,5) needs `n >= 5`.

constraints: All inputs are integers within the stated ranges

title: Goldbach Pair Count
description: For an even `n`, count the ways to write `n = p + q` with primes `p <= q`.

examples.explanation: 4 = 2 + 2 is the only way.

title: Harshad Numbers in Range
description: A positive integer is a Harshad number if it is divisible by the sum of its decimal digits. Return how many Harshad numbers lie in `[lo, hi]`.

examples.explanation: Of 10..20 the Harshad numbers are 10, 12, 18 and 20.
Every single digit number qualifies.

constraints: All inputs are integers within the stated ranges

title: Sum of Two Squares Ways
description: Return the number of pairs of integers `(a, b)` with `0 <= a <= b` and `a * a + b * b == n`.

examples.explanation: 3 cannot be written as a sum of two squares.

constraints: All inputs are integers within the stated ranges

title: Swap Adjacent Bit Pairs
description: Number the bits of `n` from 0 (least significant). Swap bit 0 with bit 1, bit 2 with bit 3, and so on for every pair, and return the resulting integer.

examples.explanation: 6 is 0110; swapping each pair gives 1001 = 9.
1 swaps into 2.

constraints: All inputs are integers within the stated ranges

title: Range XOR Total
description: Return the bitwise XOR of every integer from `l` to `r` inclusive.

examples.explanation: A single number returns itself.

constraints: All inputs are integers within the stated ranges

title: Heaviest Row or Column
description: `a` is a `rows x cols` matrix stored row by row in a flat array. Return the largest sum found among all rows and all columns.

examples.explanation: The last column sums to 3 + 6 = 9, beating every other line.
A single negative cell is both its own row and column.

title: Latin Square Check
description: `a` holds an `n x n` matrix row by row. Return `true` if every row and every column contains each integer from 1 to `n` exactly once.

examples.explanation: Each row and column is a permutation of 1..3.
The first column has two 1s.

title: Complete Graph Check
description: An undirected simple graph has `n` vertices labelled `0..n-1`. `edges` lists undirected edges as consecutive pairs: edge `i` joins `edges[2i]` and `edges[2i+1]`. Return `true` if every pair of distinct vertices is joined by an edge.

examples.explanation: All three pairs of vertices are connected.
Vertices 0 and 2 are not joined.

title: Totient Sum Up To N
description: For each `k` from 1 to `n`, let phi(k) be the count of integers in `[1, k]` that are coprime to `k`. Return the sum of phi(k) over all such `k`.

examples.explanation: Only phi(1) = 1 is counted.

constraints: All inputs are integers within the stated ranges

title: Sum of GCDs With N
description: Return the sum of `gcd(k, n)` for every integer `k` from 1 to `n`.

examples.explanation: The gcds with 6 for k = 1..6 are 1, 2, 3, 2, 1, 6.

constraints: All inputs are integers within the stated ranges

title: Modular Multiplicative Inverse
description: Return the integer `x` in `[1, m - 1]` with `(a * x) % m == 1`, or -1 if no such `x` exists.

examples.explanation: gcd(6, 9) = 3, so 6 has no inverse modulo 9.

title: Linear Congruence Solution Count
description: Return how many integers `x` in the range `[0, m - 1]` satisfy `(a * x) % m == b % m`.

examples.explanation: x = 2, 5 and 8 all give 6 * x % 9 = 3.
gcd(4, 6) = 2 does not divide 3, so no x works.

title: Two Remainder Conditions
description: Return the smallest non-negative integer `x` such that `x % m1 == a1` and `x % m2 == a2`, or -1 if no such integer exists.

examples.explanation: 8 % 3 = 2 and 8 % 5 = 3, and no smaller value works.
x would be even and odd at once, so none exists.

title: Digit Sum Divisible Count
description: Return how many integers from 1 to `n` have a digit sum that is divisible by `k`.

examples.explanation: The digit sums of 5, 14, 19, 23, 28, 32, 37, 41, 46 and 50 are multiples of 5.
With k = 1 every number from 1 to 10 qualifies.

title: Nth Digit of the Number Stream
description: Write the positive integers one after another as the infinite digit string 123456789101112... and return the `n`-th digit (1-indexed) as an integer.

examples.explanation: The stream starts 123456789101..., and the 11th digit is the 0 of 10.
The first digit is 1.

constraints: All inputs are integers within the stated ranges

title: Factorial Trailing Zeros In Base
description: Write `n!` in base `b` and return the number of trailing zero digits, which equals the largest `e` such that `b^e` divides `n!`.

examples.explanation: 10! = 3628800 ends with two zeros in base 10.
8! = 40320 = 2 * 20160 and 2^7 divides it, giving 7 zeros in base 2.

title: Smallest Number With N Divisors
description: Return the smallest positive integer that has exactly `n` positive divisors.

examples.explanation: 12 has the six divisors 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12, and no smaller number has six.
Only 1 has exactly one divisor.

constraints: The answer fits in a 32-bit signed integer

title: Flips To Make OR Match
description: In one flip you may change a single bit of `a` or of `b`. Return the minimum number of flips so that `a | b == c` afterwards.

examples.explanation: One flip sets bit 0, and clearing bit 1 in both a and b costs two more.
1 | 2 already equals 3.

constraints: All inputs are integers within the stated ranges

title: Next Integer With Same Bit Count
description: Return the smallest integer strictly greater than `n` whose binary representation has the same number of 1 bits as `n`.

examples.explanation: 6 = 110 in binary, and the next number with two set bits is 9 = 1001.
1 is followed by 2.

constraints: All inputs are integers within the stated ranges

title: Subsets Reaching Maximum OR
description: Among all non-empty subsets of `nums` (chosen by index), the largest possible bitwise OR is obtained by OR-ing every element. Return how many non-empty subsets reach that maximum OR.

examples.explanation: Only {3} and {3,1} reach the maximum OR of 3.
All 7 non-empty subsets have OR 2.

title: Shortest Max-OR Subarrays Total
description: For each start index `i`, find the length of the shortest subarray starting at `i` whose bitwise OR equals the OR of the entire suffix `nums[i..]`. Return the sum of these lengths over all `i`.

examples.explanation: The lengths are 3, 3, 2, 2 and 1, which sum to 11.
Both starts need just one element, giving 1 + 1 = 2.

title: Largest Plus Sign Order
description: `grid` is a `rows` x `cols` binary matrix. A plus sign of order `k` has a centre cell of 1 and four arms, each extending `k - 1` further cells of 1 up, down, left and right. Return the largest order of any plus sign, or 0 if the grid has no 1.

examples.explanation: The centre at row 1, column 1 has arms of length 1 in every direction, so the order is 2.
A grid with no 1 has no plus sign.

constraints: grid[i] is 0 or 1; the matrix is stored row by row in the flat array `grid` of length `rows * cols`.

title: All-Ones Submatrix Count
description: `grid` is a `rows` x `cols` binary matrix. Return the number of rectangular submatrices (of any size, at any position) in which every cell is 1.

examples.explanation: There are 6 single cells, 4 horizontal pairs... see check.
A single 1 forms exactly one submatrix.

constraints: grid[i] is 0 or 1; the matrix is stored row by row

title: Matrix Score After Flips
description: `grid` is a `rows` x `cols` binary matrix. You may flip every bit in any row or any column, as many times as you like. Read each row as a binary number (leftmost bit most significant) and return the largest possible sum of the rows.

examples.explanation: The best rows become 1111, 1001 and 1111, whose sum is 15 + 9 + 15 = 39.
The single row can be flipped to 111, which is 7.

constraints: grid[i] is 0 or 1; the matrix is stored row by row

title: Edge Closing the Cycle
description: An undirected connected graph on nodes `0..n-1` has exactly `n` edges, so removing one edge on its single cycle leaves a tree. `edges` lists undirected edges as consecutive pairs: edge `i` joins `edges[2i]` and `edges[2i+1]`. Return the 0-based index of the last edge in the list whose removal leaves a tree.

examples.explanation: The cycle is 0-1-2, and the last of its edges in the list is edge 2.
Edge 3 closes the 4-cycle and is the last cycle edge listed.

constraints: `edges.length == 2 * n`, with no repeated edges or self-loops

title: Reorient Roads To Reach Capital
description: There are `n` cities `0..n-1` joined by `n - 1` one-way roads forming a tree when directions are ignored. Road `i` runs from `edges[2i]` to `edges[2i+1]`. Return the minimum number of roads to reverse so that every city can reach city 0.

examples.explanation: Roads 0->1 and 2->3 point away from the capital... see below.
Reversing the only road 0->1 lets city 1 reach 0.

constraints: `edges.length == 2 * (n - 1)` and the roads form a tree when directions are ignored

title: Longest Dependency Chain
description: A directed acyclic graph has `n` nodes `0..n-1`; edge `i` goes from `edges[2i]` to `edges[2i+1]`. Return the number of edges on the longest directed path (0 if there are no edges).

examples.explanation: The path 0 -> 1 -> 3 -> 4 has 3 edges.
Without edges the longest path has 0 edges.

constraints: 0 <= edges.length / 2 <= 5 * 10^4, with no repeated edges or self-loops
The graph has no directed cycle

title: Knight Steps On An Infinite Board
description: A chess knight stands at `(0, 0)` on an infinite board. Return the minimum number of knight moves needed to reach the square `(x, y)`.

examples.explanation: One move reaches (2, 1).
The knight is already on the target square.

constraints: All inputs are integers within the stated ranges

title: Eventually Safe Nodes
description: In a directed graph on nodes `0..n-1`, a node is safe if every path starting at it reaches a node with no outgoing edges (a path never loops forever). Edge `i` goes from `edges[2i]` to `edges[2i+1]`. Return the number of safe nodes.

examples.explanation: Nodes 2, 4 and 5 are safe, while 0, 1 and 3 can reach the cycle 0 -> 1 -> 3... see below.
Every node ends at node 2, which has no outgoing edge.

constraints: 0 <= edges.length / 2 <= 4 * 10^4, with no repeated edges or self-loops

title: Cheapest Flight With Limited Stops
description: There are `n` cities and directed flights given in `flights` as consecutive triples `(from, to, price)`. Return the cheapest total price to travel from `src` to `dst` using at most `k` intermediate stops (so at most `k + 1` flights), or -1 if it is impossible.

examples.explanation: Going 0 -> 1 -> 3 costs 200 with one stop; the cheaper 0 -> 1 -> 2 -> 3 needs two stops.
No flight leaves city 0, so the trip is impossible.

constraints: 0 <= flights.length / 3 <= 5000, no two flights share the same (from, to), `1 <= price <= 10^4`
0 <= src, dst, k < n and src != dst

title: Signal Broadcast Time
description: A signal starts at node `k` of a directed network with `n` nodes `0..n-1` and reaches a neighbour after the edge's delay. Edges are consecutive triples `(from, to, delay)` in `times`. Return the time at which every node has received the signal, or -1 if some node never does.

examples.explanation: Node 3 is reached at time 2 via 1; every node hears by time 2.
Node 0 cannot reach node 1, so the answer is -1.

title: Longest Path In A Tree
description: An undirected tree has `n` nodes `0..n-1`. `edges` lists undirected edges as consecutive pairs: edge `i` joins `edges[2i]` and `edges[2i+1]`. Return the number of edges on the longest simple path between any two nodes.

examples.explanation: The path 3-1-0-2 has 3 edges.
A single node has no path longer than 0.

constraints: `edges.length == 2 * (n - 1)` and the edges form a tree

title: Hiking With Least Effort
description: `grid` is a `rows` x `cols` matrix of heights stored row by row. Starting at the top-left cell, you move up, down, left or right to reach the bottom-right cell. The effort of a route is the largest absolute height difference between two consecutive cells on it; return the minimum possible effort.

examples.explanation: Going 1 -> 3 -> 5 uses steps of at most 2, which beats routes with a step of 3 or more.
Every step on any route changes the height by 1... see below.

title: Numbers With All Different Digits
description: Count the integers `x` with `0 <= x < 10^n` whose decimal digits (written without leading zeros) are all different from each other.

examples.explanation: Every number below 10^2 except 11, 22, ..., 99 qualifies, giving 91.
Below 1000 exactly 739 numbers have no repeated digit.

constraints: x = 0 counts as one number with a single digit

title: Arrangements Without Adjacent Equals
description: Given `nums`, count the distinct sequences (as sequences of values) that use every element of `nums` exactly once and never place two equal values next to each other.

examples.explanation: Sequences such as [1,2,1] qualify; 1 in total.
All three values are distinct, so every one of the 6 orderings works.

title: Word Path In Letter Grid
description: `grid` is a rectangular letter board stored row by row in a string, with `cols` letters per row. Return true if `word` can be traced by moving to horizontally or vertically adjacent cells, using each cell at most once.

examples.explanation: The path a-b-c-c-e-d snakes through the board.
Reaching the second b would reuse the only b cell.

constraints: grid.length is a multiple of cols, 1 <= cols <= grid.length
1 <= word.length <= 20; all strings are lowercase letters

title: Palindrome Partition Count
description: Count the ways to cut `s` into consecutive non-empty pieces so that every piece is a palindrome. Two ways differ if their cut positions differ.

examples.explanation: Cuts a|a|b and aa|b both work.
The string is fully uniform, so every cut set works: 8.

title: Walk Over Every Empty Cell
description: `grid` is a board stored row by row with `cols` cells per row: `1` is the start, `2` is the end, `0` is a free cell and `-1` is an obstacle. Count the walks from the start to the end that move up, down, left or right and step on every non-obstacle cell exactly once.

examples.explanation: There are 2 walks that cover all non-obstacle cells.
Exactly 4 walks cover every free cell and finish at the end.

constraints: 1 <= grid.length <= 20; grid.length is a multiple of cols
grid[i] is -1, 0, 1 or 2; exactly one 1 and one 2

title: LRU Cache Replay
description: A cache holds at most `cap` keys. `ops` is a list of pairs `(key, value)`: `value = -1` means get `key` (a hit refreshes it and yields its stored value, a miss yields -1), otherwise put `value` under `key`, refreshing it and evicting the least recently used key if the cache overflows. Return the sum of all values yielded by get operations.

examples.explanation: Gets yield values that sum to 6.
Evictions turn some gets into misses, so the total is 9.

constraints: ops.length is even, at most 60; 0 <= key <= 9; value is -1 or 0..99

title: Snapshot Array Replay
description: An array of `n` zeros receives operations given as triples `(t, x, y)`: `t = 0` sets index `x` to `y`; `t = 1` takes a snapshot (`x = y = 0`) numbered 0, 1, 2, ... in order; `t = 2` reads index `x` as it was in snapshot number `y`. Return the sum of all values read.

examples.explanation: Reads see the array as of their snapshot; they sum to 5.
Later writes do not alter earlier snapshots; the reads sum to 13.

constraints: ops.length is a multiple of 3, at most 90; set values are 0..99; reads only name snapshots already taken

title: Browser History Replay
description: A browser starts on page `start`. `ops` holds pairs `(t, x)`: `t = 0` visits page `x` (discarding all forward history), `t = 1` goes back up to `x` steps, `t = 2` goes forward up to `x` steps, each stopping at the history's end. After every operation add the id of the current page to a running total, and return it.

examples.explanation: The current page after each operation sums to 18.
Moves are clamped at the ends of history; the total is 29.

constraints: ops.length is even, at most 60; visits use pages 1..9; back/forward steps are 0..10

title: Memory Allocator Replay
description: A memory of `n` units starts free. `ops` holds triples: `(0, size, id)` places `size` units under `id` in the leftmost run of consecutive free units that fits and yields its starting index (or -1 if none fits); `(1, id, 0)` frees every unit owned by `id` and yields how many were freed. Return the sum of all yielded values.

examples.explanation: Allocations take the leftmost fitting gap; yielded values sum to 20.
Freed gaps are reused by later allocations; the total is 10.

constraints: ops.length is a multiple of 3, at most 90; ids are 1..9, 1 <= size <= n; an id may be reused

title: Ring Rotation Checksum
description: `grid` stores a `rows` by `cols` matrix row by row. Treat each concentric border ring as a loop and rotate every ring counter-clockwise by `k` single steps (each value moves to the next cell counter-clockwise). Return the sum of `(i + 1) * v` over the final row-major array, where `v` is the value at flat index `i`.

examples.explanation: Rotating the single ring once gives a checksum of 25.
The two rings rotate independently; the checksum is 1292.

constraints: 2 <= rows, cols <= 20; min(rows, cols) is even; 0 <= grid[i] <= 100

title: Primitive Triple Count
description: Count the triples `(a, b, c)` of positive integers with `a < b`, `a^2 + b^2 = c^2`, `gcd(a, b, c) = 1` and `c <= n`.

examples.explanation: Euclid pairs with hypotenuse at most the limit number 1.
Counting primitive triples up to this limit gives 11.

constraints: a, b, c are positive integers

title: Dominant AND Pairs
description: Count the index pairs `i < j` for which `nums[i] & nums[j]` is strictly greater than `nums[i] ^ nums[j]`.

examples.explanation: Pairs sharing their highest set bit qualify; there are 2.
Only pairs with equal top bits count, giving 0.

title: Topological Orderings Count
description: A directed graph has `n` nodes `0..n-1`, and `edges` lists arcs as consecutive pairs `u, v` (arc `u -> v`). Count the orderings of all nodes in which every arc's tail appears before its head; the count is 0 if the graph has a cycle.

examples.explanation: Exactly 2 orderings respect every arc.
The result for this graph is 0.

constraints: 0 <= edges.length / 2 <= 40; no self-loops or repeated arcs

title: Mini Sudoku Completions
description: `grid` holds a 4x4 sudoku row by row (16 numbers; `0` means empty). A completed grid has digits 1-4 exactly once in every row, every column and each of the four 2x2 corner blocks. Count the ways to fill the empty cells so the grid is complete (0 if the given digits already conflict).

examples.explanation: The given digits leave 1 valid completions.
This grid has 288 valid completions.

title: Expression Targets Count
description: Between the digits of `num` you may place `+`, `-`, `*` or nothing (gluing neighbouring digits into one multi-digit number; a number may not start with `0` unless it is just `0`). Count the distinct operator choices whose expression evaluates to `target` with the usual precedence of `*` over `+`/`-`.

examples.explanation: 2 operator placements reach the target.
Exactly 2 placements evaluate to the target.

title: Walks Of Length K Between Nodes
description: A directed graph has `n` nodes `0..n-1`, and `edges` lists arcs as consecutive pairs `u, v` (arc `u -> v`). Count the walks that start at `s`, end at `t` and use exactly `k` arcs (nodes and arcs may repeat), modulo 1000000007.

examples.explanation: Walks of exactly 2 arcs from 0 to 2 number 1.
Counting walks of the stated length gives 0.

constraints: 0 <= edges.length / 2 <= 60; no self-loops or repeated arcs

title: Hamiltonian Path Count
description: An undirected graph has `n` nodes `0..n-1`, and `edges` lists edges as consecutive pairs `u, v`. Count the paths that visit every node exactly once; a path and its reverse are the same path, and a single node counts as one path.

examples.explanation: Exactly 1 paths pass through every node once.
This graph has 0 Hamiltonian paths.

constraints: 0 <= edges.length / 2 <= 66; no self-loops or repeated edges

title: Fewest Colors For Graph
description: An undirected graph has `n` nodes `0..n-1`, and `edges` lists edges as consecutive pairs `u, v`. Return the smallest number of colors needed to color every node so that the two ends of each edge get different colors.

examples.explanation: The graph can be colored with 3 colors and no fewer.
The minimum number of colors is 2.

constraints: 0 <= edges.length / 2 <= 66; no self-loops or repeated edges

title: Minimum Path Cover In DAG
description: A directed acyclic graph has `n` nodes `0..n-1`, and `edges` lists arcs as consecutive pairs `u, v` (arc `u -> v`). Return the fewest paths, following arcs and sharing no node, needed so that every node lies on exactly one path (a single node is a path).

examples.explanation: The nodes can be split into 1 vertex-disjoint paths at best.
The fewest vertex-disjoint paths covering all nodes is 3.

constraints: 0 <= edges.length / 2 <= 100; no self-loops or repeated arcs; the graph is acyclic

title: Pascal Row Non-Multiples
description: Row `n` of Pascal's triangle holds the binomial coefficients C(n, 0), C(n, 1), ..., C(n, n). Given a prime `p`, count the entries in row `n` that are not divisible by `p`.

examples.explanation: Row n has 2 entries that are not multiples of p.
Counting non-multiples of p in the row gives 4.

constraints: p is a prime with 2 <= p <= 1000

title: Smallest Power Hitting Residue
description: Find the smallest integer `x >= 0` such that `a^x` leaves the same remainder as `b` when divided by `m` (with `a^0 = 1`), or return -1 if there is none. `a` and `m` need not be coprime.

examples.explanation: The smallest exponent that works is 3.
The answer for this triple is -1.

title: Last Nonzero Digit Of Factorial
description: Return the last digit of `n!` (n factorial) that is not zero, i.e. the last digit after stripping all trailing zeros.

examples.explanation: The last nonzero digit of n! is 2.
Stripping the trailing zeros leaves a final digit of 8.

constraints: n! is far too large to compute directly for big n

title: Rotation Distinct Necklaces
description: A circular necklace has `n` beads, each painted with one of `k` colors. Two necklaces count as the same if one can be rotated to match the other (reflections are different); return the number of distinct necklaces modulo 1000000007.

examples.explanation: Up to rotation there are 4 distinct necklaces.
Counting rotation classes gives 6.

title: Prime Digit Sum Without Thirteen
description: Given the decimal string `n`, count the integers `x` with `1 <= x <= n` whose digit sum is a prime number and whose decimal form does not contain the substring "13".

examples.explanation: Exactly 9 integers up to n qualify.
Qualifying integers up to n number 37.

constraints: `n` is the decimal form of an integer with no leading zeros

title: Domino Tilings Of Four-Row Strip
description: Count the ways to tile a board with 4 rows and `n` columns using 1x2 and 2x1 dominoes so that every cell is covered exactly once, modulo 1000000007.

examples.explanation: A 4 x n board can be tiled in 1 ways.
The tiling count is 5.

title: Distant Term Of A Recurrence
description: A sequence satisfies `a[i] = coeffs[0]*a[i-1] + coeffs[1]*a[i-2] + ... + coeffs[d-1]*a[i-d]` for `i >= d`, where `d = coeffs.length`, and its first `d` terms are given by `init`. Return `a[k]` modulo 1000000007 (0-indexed).

examples.explanation: These coefficients give a[k] = 55 modulo 1000000007.
The requested term is 21.

title: Proper Colorings Count
description: An undirected graph has `n` nodes `0..n-1`, and `edges` lists edges as consecutive pairs `u, v`. Count the ways to give every node one of `k` colors so that the endpoints of every edge differ, modulo 1000000007.

examples.explanation: The graph has 6 proper colorings.
Valid colorings number 2 modulo 1000000007.

constraints: 0 <= edges.length / 2 <= 66; no self-loops or repeated edges

title: Global Minimum Cut Weight
description: A weighted undirected graph has `n` nodes `0..n-1`, and `edges` lists edges as consecutive triples `u, v, w`. Split the nodes into two non-empty groups so that the total weight of edges crossing between them is as small as possible, and return that total (0 if the graph is disconnected).

examples.explanation: The lightest cut separating the nodes has weight 3.
The minimum cut weight is 10.

constraints: 0 <= edges.length / 3 <= 200; 1 <= w <= 100; no self-loops or repeated node pairs

title: Cheapest One-To-One Assignment
description: `cost` is an `n x n` matrix stored row by row in a flat array, where `cost[i*n + j]` is the price of giving task `j` to worker `i`. Assign every worker a different task and return the smallest possible total price.

examples.explanation: The cheapest complete assignment costs 5.
Best one-to-one assignment total is 5.

title: Kth Smallest Subset XOR
description: Consider the XOR of every subset of `nums` (the empty subset gives 0), so there are `2^n` values counted with multiplicity. Return the `k`-th smallest of these values in sorted order, with `k` counted from 1.

examples.explanation: The k-th smallest subset XOR is 2.
Sorting all subset XORs puts 0 at position k.

title: Falling Squares Height Total
description: `squares` lists squares as consecutive pairs `left, side`. Squares are dropped one by one onto a line; each occupies `[left, left+side)` horizontally and falls until it rests on the highest earlier square it overlaps (touching only at an edge is not an overlap) or on the ground. After each drop take the height of the tallest stack so far, and return the sum of these heights.

examples.explanation: Summing the tallest-stack height after every drop gives 12.
The running maximum heights add up to 200.

title: Range Module Replay
description: A range tracker starts empty and `ops` lists operations as consecutive triples `t, l, r` on the half-open range `[l, r)`: `t = 0` starts tracking every real number in it, `t = 1` stops tracking every real number in it, and `t = 2` is a query asking whether every real number in it is currently tracked. Return the sum of `i + 1` over all query operations (0-indexed operation `i`) that answer true.

examples.explanation: The true queries have operation numbers summing to 12 (1-based).
Adding up i + 1 for true queries gives 0.

constraints: 3 <= ops.length <= 30000 and ops.length is a multiple of 3

title: Max Stack Replay
description: A stack supports operations given as consecutive pairs `t, x` in `ops`: `t = 0` pushes `x`; `t = 1` pops and returns the top; `t = 2` returns the top without removing it; `t = 3` returns the largest value; `t = 4` removes and returns the largest value (the topmost one if it appears several times). For `t != 0`, `x` is always 0. Return the sum of `(i + 1) * result` over every operation `i` (0-indexed) that returns a value, modulo 1000000007.

examples.explanation: Weighting each returned value by its 1-based operation number gives 82.
The weighted sum of returned values is 14.

constraints: 0 <= x <= 10^6 for pushes; no operation is applied to an empty stack

title: Subsets With Zero AND
description: Count the non-empty subsets of `nums` (chosen by index, so equal values at different positions are different choices) whose bitwise AND is exactly 0. Return the count modulo 1000000007.

examples.explanation: Exactly 1 subsets have an AND of zero.
The number of zero-AND subsets is 1.

title: Lattice Floor Sum
description: Compute the sum of `floor((a*i + b) / m)` for `i = 0, 1, ..., n-1`, modulo 1000000007.

examples.explanation: The floors add up to 3 modulo 1000000007.
The requested sum is 0.

title: Fewest Squares To Tile Rectangle
description: Cover an `n x m` rectangle exactly with axis-aligned squares of integer side lengths, with no overlaps and no gaps. Return the smallest number of squares needed.

examples.explanation: The rectangle can be covered by at least 3 squares.
The minimum square count is 1.

title: Eulerian Circuit Count
description: A directed graph has `n` nodes `0..n-1`, and `edges` lists arcs as consecutive pairs `u, v` (arc `u -> v`). Count the distinct Eulerian circuits: closed walks that use every arc exactly once. Circuits that differ only by where they start are the same circuit; return 0 if none exist.

examples.explanation: The arcs form 1 distinct Eulerian circuits.
Counting circuits that use every arc once gives 1.

constraints: 2 <= edges.length / 2 <= 16; no self-loops or repeated arcs

title: Maximum Matching In General Graph
description: An undirected graph (not necessarily bipartite) has `n` nodes `0..n-1`, and `edges` lists edges as consecutive pairs `u, v`. Return the largest number of edges that can be chosen so that no node is an endpoint of two chosen edges.

examples.explanation: At most 2 disjoint edges can be chosen.
The maximum matching has 1 edges.

constraints: 0 <= edges.length / 2 <= 200; no self-loops or repeated edges

title: Cheapest Rooted Spanning Arborescence
description: A directed graph has `n` nodes `0..n-1`, and `edges` lists weighted arcs as consecutive triples `u, v, w` (arc `u -> v` of cost `w`). Choose arcs so that every node can be reached from `root` by exactly one path of chosen arcs (each non-root node has exactly one chosen incoming arc and the root has none). Return the smallest total cost, or -1 if impossible.

examples.explanation: The cheapest arborescence from the root costs 8.
The minimum total arc cost is -1.

constraints: 0 <= edges.length / 3 <= 200; 1 <= w <= 100; no self-loops or repeated (u, v) arcs

title: Smallest Modular Square Root
description: Given a prime `p` and an integer `a`, find the smallest `x` with `0 <= x < p` such that `x*x` leaves the same remainder as `a` when divided by `p`, or return -1 if no such `x` exists.

examples.explanation: The smallest square root of a modulo p is 3.
The result for this pair is -1.

constraints: p is a prime with 2 <= p <= 10^9
